common_name: Angelface White Angelonia (Pure White Large-Flowered Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost once soil has warmed; this clean white selection is a straightforward color companion to the purple, blue, and pink Angelface entries already in this dataset.

directions: Angelface White carries pure white, extra-large snapdragon-like blooms on the same dense, semi-upright, well-branched frame shared across the Angelface line, giving growers a bright neutral to pair with the series' blues and pinks. It self-cleans without deadheading and keeps producing new flowering stems from spring through the first fall frost, including through the hottest, muggiest weeks of summer that stall many bedding annuals. Plant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun after frost danger passes, pinch young plants once to build a fuller shape, and feed on a regular schedule to sustain the long bloom season.

common_name: Angelface Perfectly Pink Angelonia (Vivid Pink Large-Flowered Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost into full sun once nights have warmed; this vivid pink selection fills a color gap left by the blue- and purple-leaning Angelface entries already cataloged.

directions: Angelface Perfectly Pink produces saturated, vivid pink flowers noticeably larger than older seed-grown angelonia, carried on a semi-upright, well-branched habit typical of the Angelface line. Deer tend to leave it alone, and the plant tolerates both brief waterlogging and stretches of drought without losing bloom quality. It flowers non-stop from spring through frost with no deadheading needed, holding up through the punishing heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer that causes true snapdragons to collapse. A single early pinch encourages denser branching, and steady feeding keeps the heavy flower count going all season.

common_name: Angelface Cascade Blue Angelonia (Trailing Blue Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost into hanging baskets, window boxes, or the edge of raised containers, since Cascade's low, trailing habit is bred for spilling rather than upright bedding use.

directions: Unlike the upright, mounding habit of most Angelface colors, Cascade Blue spreads sideways and drapes over a container edge, functioning as a trailing spiller rather than a thriller in mixed plantings. Its blue flower spikes appear continuously from spring through frost without deadheading, and the plant shares the series' strong resistance to summer heat, humidity, and the diseases that trouble many container annuals in wet weather. Grow it in full sun in a well-drained container mix, and let it dry slightly between waterings to keep growth compact rather than stretched. Light fertilizing every few weeks sustains bloom through the hottest months.
sources: Penn State Extension Flower Trial Gardens

common_name: Angelface Cascade Snow Angelonia (Trailing White Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost into hanging baskets or container edges; Cascade Snow is the white counterpart to Cascade Blue within the same trailing sub-line of the Angelface series.

directions: Cascade Snow carries the same low, spreading Cascade habit as Cascade Blue but in bright white, making it a natural trailing filler for baskets and window boxes rather than a bedding plant. It self-cleans without deadheading and keeps flowering from spring through frost, tolerating the heat and humidity spikes that reduce bloom in cool-season spike flowers like snapdragon. Grow in full sun in a well-drained container mix, water when the top inch dries, and expect the trailing stems to fill in and drape over the container rim within a few weeks of transplanting. Feed lightly on a regular schedule to keep the long cascading stems in full flower.

common_name: AngelMist Spreading White Angelonia (Low Mounding Trailing Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost into containers, hanging baskets, or as a low filler at bed edges; unlike most AngelMist colors this selection spreads wide rather than growing upright.

directions: AngelMist Spreading White grows wide and low rather than upright, sweeping sideways to fill gaps in a bed or drape over a container edge without smothering neighboring plants. Flowering happens continuously on new growth, so the plant never stops pushing fresh stems and blooms until frost, matching the exceptional heat, humidity, and drought tolerance of the rest of the AngelMist line. It needs no pinching or deadheading to maintain a full, tidy shape, and performs best in full sun with soil that dries slightly between waterings rather than staying constantly wet. Use it as a spiller in combination containers or as a groundcover-like filler along a sunny border.
sources: Penn State Extension Flower Trial Gardens

common_name: AngelMist Purple Improved Angelonia (Vigorous Upright Purple Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost into well-drained beds or large containers; this improved selection was bred for stronger branching and better flower coverage than earlier purple AngelMist stock.

directions: Purple Improved refines the original AngelMist purple with denser branching and heavier flower coverage, producing tall spikes of deep purple, orchid-like blooms over glossy, narrow foliage. It shares the vigorous, well-filled vegetative habit that distinguishes AngelMist from seed-grown angelonia series, holding form and color through the hottest, most humid stretch of a Gulf Coast summer. Plant in well-drained soil in full sun after frost danger passes, and expect strong drought tolerance once roots are established, with almost no deadheading required since spent flowers are inconspicuous along the spike. Occasional light feeding keeps the extended bloom period going from early summer to frost.

common_name: AngelMist Deep Plum Angelonia (Burgundy-Flowered Vigorous Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost into well-drained, richly amended soil; Deep Plum's burgundy tone gives the AngelMist series a darker color option than its purples, pinks, and whites.

directions: Deep Plum stands out from the rest of the AngelMist palette with rich burgundy flower spikes over semi-evergreen, deep green foliage, adding a moodier color choice to plantings otherwise dominated by purples, pinks, and whites. Bees and butterflies visit it readily, and the plant handles both heat and humidity with the same ease as the rest of the vigorous, vegetatively propagated AngelMist line. Grow in rich, well-drained soil in full sun with occasional deep watering, letting the soil dry between waterings once plants are established. No deadheading is needed, and light, regular feeding keeps flower production strong from early summer through the first frost.

common_name: Serena Lavender Angelonia (Soft Lavender Compact Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 plant March-May. Serena Lavender rounds out the seed-grown Serena color range with a soft pastel tone alongside the purple, blue, and white Serena entries already cataloged here.

directions: Serena Lavender offers a gentler, pastel option within the compact, uniform Serena breeding line, softening the color palette next to the more saturated Serena Purple and Serena Blue. The apple-scented, deep green foliage and well-branched, self-cleaning habit are typical of the series, producing fragrant flower spikes without any deadheading needed. It is deer- and rabbit-resistant and holds up to both drought and the intense heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer that stalls many cool-season bedding flowers. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and water moderately through establishment, then only as the top inch of soil dries.

common_name: Serenita Lavender Angelonia (True Lavender Compact Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 8-9 plant March-May. Serenita Lavender flowers about a week earlier than its Serenita Lavender Pink sibling and needs less growth regulation than the taller seed-grown Serena line.

directions: Serenita Lavender delivers a true, clear lavender flower color on the naturally compact, mounded Serenita habit, filling out a pack or container without pinching. It reaches flowering roughly a week ahead of the closely related Serenita Lavender Pink and produces strong secondary flushes after the first bloom cycle. Like the rest of the Serenita line it is self-cleaning, drought-tolerant once established, and largely untouched by deer and rabbits, thriving through the same summer heat and humidity that cause true snapdragons to fail. Grow in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, watering only as the surface dries.

common_name: Serenita Lavender Pink Angelonia (Bicolor Lavender-Pink Compact Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 8-9 plant March-May. Flowering follows about a week behind the solid-toned Serenita Lavender within the same compact series.

directions: Serenita Lavender Pink blends soft lavender and pink tones on each small snapdragon-like bloom, giving this Serenita color more visual complexity than the solid lavender of its series-mate. The compact, well-branched, mounded habit needs no pinching to fill a container or bed position, and spent flowers drop cleanly without deadheading. It shares the Serenita line's strong drought tolerance and near-immunity to deer and rabbit browsing, plus the same ability to keep flowering through the peak heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, watering deeply but infrequently once plants are established.

common_name: Serenita Purple Angelonia (Compact Purple Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 8-9 plant March-May. Serenita Purple gives the compact Serenita series a deep purple option alongside its pink, sky blue, and lavender series-mates already cataloged here.

directions: Serenita Purple produces deep purple flower spikes on the same naturally compact, uniform, self-branching frame shared across the Serenita series, filling out a pot or bed position without pinching. It requires little to no growth regulation compared with the taller, seed-grown Serena line, making it easier to keep tidy in commercial production and home gardens alike. The plant is self-cleaning, deer- and rabbit-resistant, and blooms continuously from late spring through frost despite the heat and humidity that stress cool-season spike flowers. Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and water only as the top inch dries.

common_name: Serenita White Angelonia (Compact White Summer Snapdragon)

planting.note: Set out transplants after all frost danger has passed when soil is warm; in zone 8-9 plant March-May. Serenita White completes the compact Serenita line's neutral end alongside its pink, purple, sky blue, and lavender counterparts.

directions: Serenita White brings a clean, bright white to the compact Serenita series, pairing easily with almost any other bedding or container color in the line. Its tidy, mounded, well-branched habit fills out quickly without pinching, and the plant is largely self-cleaning, dropping spent flowers without leaving visible dead blooms. Like its series-mates it tolerates deer and rabbit browsing pressure poorly for the pests and well for the gardener, and it keeps flowering through the intense heat and humidity of a long Gulf Coast summer. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil, watering deeply but infrequently once established.
